items.title: [isomorphic-git] isomorphic-git allows unbounded memory allocation from attacker-controlled delta target size (DoS)
items.summary: SummaryWhen applying a delta object from a packfile, isomorphic-git reads a server-controlled targetSize and calls Buffer.alloc(targetSize) with no upper bound. A single malicious HTTP response to git.clone()/git.fetch() can force a ~2 GB allocation → memory exhaustion / DoS (process killed on memory-constrained hosts).Detailssrc/utils/applyDelta.js:const sourceSize = readVarIntLE(reader)const targetSize = readVarIntLE(reader)   // attacker-controlled…target = Buffer.alloc(targetSize)A pack with one OBJ_REF_DELTA whose header declares targetSize = 0x7FFFFFFF (~2 GB) and a 1-byte op causes the full allocation up front. The subsequent size-mismatch error is swallowed in GitPackIndex.fromPack, so on a host with spare RAM it silently wastes ~2 GB; on a small host the OS SIGKILLs the process.Canonical git behavior (divergence)git rejects the same 78-byte pack in ~96 ms — error: delta replay has gone wild / fatal: … failed to apply delta — with no large allocation and no hang (it bounds delta replay against the declared size rather than trusting it).PoChttps://github.com/spiceoverflow/av4-oom — open in a Codespace; a single clone/fetch against the bundled server, run under --max-old-space-size=256:[AV-4] *** OOM ALLOCATION CONFIRMED — Buffer.alloc(targetSize) RAN ***[AV-4] External (Buffer) memory rose by 2048 MB during clone.(The allocation is off-heap, so a Node heap cap does not mitigate it.)ImpactA denial of service via unbounded memory allocation: a single response from a malicious or MitM'd server to git.clone()/git.fetch() forces a multi-gigabyte allocation, crashing the process on memory-constrained hosts.Any application or service that clones or fetches from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git — most acutely containers, serverless functions, and small VMs, where the OS OOM-kills the process.Suggested fixDon't pre-allocate the untrusted targetSize: build the result from the actual delta ops and validate the total against targetSize before concatenating (and/or cap it against the advertised pack size).Referenceshttps://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/security/advisories/GHSA-9x82-4j54-863hhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63476https://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/pull/2370https://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/pull/2373https://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/commit/5c37ea69e9691183fc52d41ba7b6361263e9feddhttps://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/commit/823843d1cd19182df79bc907c767f5bcecb39a0bhttps://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/releases/tag/v1.38.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9x82-4j54-863h

items.title: [i18next] i18next deepExtend recurses into inherited built-ins, allowing corruption of shared built-in objects (DoS)
items.summary: SummarydeepExtend in src/utils.js (reached via the public addResourceBundle(lng, ns, data, deep, overwrite) API) checked key existence with the in operator, which walks the prototype chain. A source key matching an inherited built-in (e.g. hasOwnProperty, toString, valueOf) therefore caused the function to recurse into the shared object on Object.prototype. With overwrite: true, a nested value could overwrite a property of that shared built-in — for example setting Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call to a non-callable value — corrupting it process-wide and causing an unrecoverable denial of service.This is distinct from CVE-2026-48713 (i18next-fs-backend) and CVE-2026-48714 (i18next-http-middleware), which are prototype pollution via setPath/key-walking in different packages. This issue is in i18next core, via a different mechanism (the in operator in deepExtend), and is gated behind a non-default call configuration.Detailssrc/utils.js (≤ 26.3.3):export const deepExtend = (target, source, overwrite) => {  for (const prop in source) {    if (prop !== '__proto__' && prop !== 'constructor') {      if (prop in target) {            // <-- walks the prototype chain        if (isString(target[prop]) || target[prop] instanceof String ||            isString(source[prop]) || source[prop] instanceof String) {          if (overwrite) target[prop] = source[prop];        } else {          deepExtend(target[prop], source[prop], overwrite);        }      } else {        target[prop] = source[prop];      }    }  }  return target;};For source = { hasOwnProperty: { call: "corrupted" } } and target = {}: "hasOwnProperty" in target is true (inherited from Object.prototype), so the code recurses with target = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty. In that call, "call" in target is true (inherited from Function.prototype), source.call is a string, and with overwrite: true the assignment sets an own call property on Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty to the string "corrupted". Every subsequent Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(...) then throws TypeError, including i18next's own internals.The existing __proto__/constructor guard does not cover this, because the corruption target is an inherited built-in function, not the prototype object itself.Proof of Conceptimport i18next from 'i18next';await i18next.init({ lng: 'en', resources: { en: { translation: {} } } });const payload = { hasOwnProperty: { call: 'corrupted' } };i18next.addResourceBundle('en', 'translation', payload, /* deep */ true, /* overwrite */ true);// Process-wide corruption:Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call({}, 'test'); // TypeError: ... is not a functionImpactDenial of service (process-wide, unrecoverable) and limited integrity impact (a shared built-in property is set to an attacker-supplied value).Preconditions (why severity is Medium, not High): the application must pass attacker-controlled data into addResourceBundle with both deep: true and overwrite: true. No standard i18next backend or integration does this; it only occurs in explicit application code that merges untrusted content. The default addResourceBundle path (no deep merge, or overwrite falsy) is not affected.PatchFixed in i18next 26.3.4 by checking existence with Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, prop) instead of the in operator, so inherited keys are copied as plain own data instead of triggering recursion.Referenceshttps://github.com/i18next/i18next/security/advisories/GHSA-6jcc-5g8w-32mxhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63402https://github.com/i18next/i18next/commit/642137b7786d83661ec3ee53027798dc4b81d30ahttps://github.com/i18next/i18next/releases/tag/v26.3.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6jcc-5g8w-32mx

items.title: [xo-server] Xen Orchestra: Empty-object login token
items.summary: SummaryREST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}. REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string. The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs.DetailsIn packages/xo-server/src/api/session.mjs, function  signIn(credentials) has no params schema (unlike the deprecated signInWithToken, which declares token: { type: 'string' }), so credentials.token can be any JSON value.packages/xo-server/src/xo-mixins/authentication.mjs, token provider:this.registerAuthenticationProvider(async ({ token: tokenId }, { ip } = {}) => {  if (!tokenId) return          // {} is truthy → passes  const token = await app.getAuthenticationToken(tokenId)  ...  return { bypassOtp: true, expiration: token.expiration, userId: token.user_id }getAuthenticationToken(properties) explicitly accepts an object, and _getAuthenticationToken(id, properties) does this._tokens.first(properties ?? id).Collection#first(properties) -> _get(properties); in collection/redis.mjs, if (isEmpty(properties)) return redis.sMembers(prefix + '_ids')… → all tokens. Non-empty objects on indexed fields (user_id, client_id) do an index lookup → token of the chosen user.HTTP paths: index.mjs (req.cookies.token → isValidAuthenticationToken), xo-mixins/rest-api.mjs and @xen-orchestra/rest-api middleware (cookies.authenticationToken ?? cookies.token → authenticateUser({ token })). cookie-parser turns j:-prefixed cookie values into parsed JSON, so authenticationToken=j:{} yields {}.Proof of conceptThe object cookie returned 200 with unexpired token IDs, and one ID worked on a fresh request as an admin account. The attacker does not choose which token the empty-object lookup returns. Authentication succeeds only if the token returned first is unexpired and belongs to an existing user; if it is expired or its user was deleted, the request fails without trying another token.curl -b 'authenticationToken=j:{}' https://<ip>/rest/v0/usersImpactAn adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.Referenceshttps://github.com/vatesfr/xen-orchestra/security/advisories/GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5ghttps://github.com/vatesfr/xen-orchestra/pull/10748https://github.com/vatesfr/xen-orchestra/commit/50166fe3a49c02069d35ba9046ca4a1f77f4e11dhttps://docs.vates.tech/security-advisories/advisories/2026/vates-sa-2026-062https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5g
